questions.q: What is the real practice this lesson describes for verifying a newly deployed network?
options: Deploy one disposable test VM/instance per tier and confirm what should and shouldn't be reachable
Assume the NSG/security group rules work because they were written correctly in Lesson 7
Wait until Chapter 3's real compute is deployed, then check connectivity
Only check that the web tier can reach the internet, since that's the most visible tier
questions.explain: Deploying a small test resource into each tier and testing actual connectivity closes the gap between a rule looking correct and being correct.

questions.q: Why does verification need to check both positive and negative cases?
options: Because confirming allowed traffic works is not enough — you also have to confirm disallowed traffic is actually blocked
Because cloud providers require two separate test VMs per subnet
Negative checks are optional and only needed for compliance audits
Positive checks are unnecessary once negative checks pass
questions.explain: A network can correctly allow web traffic to the internet while an NSG mistake also leaves the data tier wrongly reachable — both directions need testing.

questions.q: What do Azure Network Watcher and AWS Reachability Analyzer provide beyond a simple ping or port test?
options: They trace a specific network path and report exactly which rule allowed or blocked it
They automatically fix any misconfigured NSG or security group rule
They replace the need to deploy any test VM at all
They only work after a production incident has already occurred
questions.explain: Both tools trace the actual path through NSGs/security groups and route tables, identifying the specific rule responsible for an allow or a block.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is catching a network misconfiguration during this verification step cheaper than catching it later?
options: Fixing it now means editing one rule and redeploying a test VM; catching it after Chapter 3's real resources are deployed means a real database may have been exposed and an incident write-up is needed
There is no real cost difference — both situations require the same amount of work
Fixing it later is actually cheaper because the real workload provides better diagnostic information
Network misconfigurations can only be fixed before any compute is deployed at all
questions.explain: The fix itself is the same edit either way, but catching it early avoids exposing real production data and avoids the incident response work.

questions.q: What happens to the test VM/instance used to verify connectivity in this lesson?
options: It's disposable — used only to test the real NSG/security group rules before deploying the actual workload
It becomes the production web server for the environment
It's kept permanently as a monitoring endpoint
It replaces the need for an NSG or security group on that subnet
questions.explain: The test VM exists only to put the actual deployed rules under a real test, not to serve as part of the production environment.
